design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (tabulation and vote counting) of randomized trials of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD, said to follow PRISMA, not registered and without a protocol (Journal of Psychoactive Drugs, online 2025, pp. 1–13). CINAHL, PubMed, Medline, PsycInfo and the Cochrane Library were searched in March 2023 with keywords for clinical trials published in peer-reviewed journals in 2002–2022, and the search was rerun in May 2025. Six trials were analysed (two pilot trials, two phase 2 dose-response trials and the two phase 3 trials; 280 participants), all linked to MAPS; two pooled analyses retracted in August 2024 and one long-term follow-up were tabulated but excluded. Outcomes summarised: CAPS change and loss of diagnosis at each trial's primary end point, long-term follow-up, adverse events, suicidality, blinding and other limitations, and dropout.
can_establish: Which randomized trials of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD were found in the databases searched up to May 2025, and how the authors summarised their direction of effect, adverse events, suicidality, blinding and dropout.
cannot_establish: A pooled effect size or its uncertainty (no meta-analysis); a validated risk-of-bias appraisal of the trials (no tool was used); anything outside the trial publications (no registries, regulatory documents or grey literature); and, because of transcription errors, the trial numbers themselves, which should be taken from the trial reports.

sample.recruitment: Database search (see design), run by a librarian as non-financial support; titles and abstracts screened independently by two reviewers (Methods, p. 2; Other information, p. 10).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized controlled trial design, PTSD treatment condition and MDMA-AT (Methods, p. 2). Of the 26 records, 14 were eliminated (6 on mechanisms in healthy controls, 6 outside the scope, 1 not specific to MDMA-AT, 1 abstract only); the 2025 rerun added one article (Mitchell et al., 2023). Of the 13 articles so identified, four more were eliminated: three for focusing on secondary outcomes (Ching et al., 2022; Nicholas et al., 2022; Ponte et al., 2021) and one randomized trial (Bouso et al., 2008) for outcome measures inconsistent with the others, in part because it was conducted outside the United States, so that all analysed trials used the CAPS. Two retracted pooled analyses (Mithoefer et al., 2019; Jerome et al., 2020) and a long-term follow-up overlapping another trial (Mithoefer et al., 2013) were then left out of the analysis (p. 2).
sample.demographics: Analysed trials: mean age 37.2 to 42.0 years; 66.4% female; baseline CAPS thresholds from 28 or more to 50 or more; three trials with an inactive placebo and three with low-dose MDMA as an active placebo; four of six trials 90% to 100% White, the two phase 3 trials more diverse (p. 3; p. 8; Tables 1 and 5).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; the review reports dropout of 7.1% to 16.7% in the trials (p. 8).
sample.selection_effects: Peer-reviewed journals only (2002–2022 in the first search), five databases, no trial registries, regulatory documents, reference-list searches or grey literature; one randomized trial excluded after the fact for its outcome measure. Every trial found, including the excluded Bouso et al. (2008), which lists the MAPS founder among its authors, is linked to MAPS, so the review cannot speak to independent evidence. Table 1 lists six phase 2 registrations under the pooled analyses, two of which (NCT01958593, the trial at the site of the ethical violation, and NCT01689740) correspond to no analysed study; the review does not say whether their results were sought.

exposure.measurement: As tabulated from the trial reports: MDMA in two or three experimental sessions with MAPS-manualized therapy, against an inactive placebo (three trials) or low-dose MDMA as an active placebo (three trials) (p. 3; Table 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as tabulated (Table 1, p. 3): initial active doses of 75, 100 or 125 mg in the phase 2 and pilot trials, with low-dose MDMA of 25, 30 or 40 mg as active placebo; the two phase 3 trials are listed only by the first session's initial dose of 80 mg, whereas the trial reports give 80 mg in session 1 and 120 mg in sessions 2 and 3, each followed by a supplemental half-dose. The text counts the 160 active-dose participants as those given an initial dose of 40 mg or more, a threshold that would include the 40 mg active-placebo arm, which the 160 excludes (editors' sum of Table 1); Table 2 gives that active placebo as 30 mg; the Appendix gives 80–120 mg per session for MAPP1 (pp. 3, 4, 13).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, beyond noting that MAPP2 excluded substance use disorders other than mild cannabis or alcohol use (Appendix, p. 13).

comparison.controls: Inactive placebo (Mithoefer et al., 2011; Mitchell et al., 2021, 2023) or low-dose MDMA as an active placebo (Oehen et al., 2013; Ot'alora et al., 2018; Mithoefer et al., 2018), with the same therapy in both arms (p. 3).

outcomes.instruments: CAPS (CAPS-IV or CAPS-5) change at each trial's primary end point; proportion no longer meeting PTSD criteria; long-term follow-up; adverse events as each trial reported them (different instruments and time windows); C-SSRS suicidality; blinding (correct guesses), sample size, diversity, conflicts of interest and bias-reduction steps; dropout (pp. 2–8; Tables 2–5).
outcomes.validity_norms: The review notes that adverse-event reporting varied substantially between trials and measures, making synthesis difficult (p. 4; p. 9).
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy is the number of trials with a statistically significant CAPS difference (vote counting) and the range of loss-of-diagnosis percentages; no effect sizes are pooled or tabulated.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests were done. The count of 6 covers CAPS change, loss of diagnosis, long-term follow-up, adverse events, suicidality and dropout.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; each trial's blinding is tabulated (Table 5).

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled and no confidence intervals. Vote count: 5 of 6 trials found a significantly greater CAPS decrease with MDMA; Oehen et al. (2013) did not reach significance (p = 0.0666, Appendix p. 12). Loss of diagnosis at the primary end point: 41.7% to 85.7% in active-dose arms vs 25.0% to 33.3% in placebo arms, excluding Oehen et al. (2013), in which all 12 participants still met criteria (p. 4; Table 2). Long-term follow-up: 41.6% to 100% no longer meeting criteria (p. 4). Dropout 7.1% to 16.7% (p. 8).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The authors state that the review was not registered and no protocol was prepared (Other information, p. 10).
analysis.selective_reporting: The placebo-arm loss-of-diagnosis results of the two phase 3 trials are not tabulated (Table 2, p. 4), and the stated placebo range omits MAPP2's 47.6% (20 of 42); serious, severe and special-interest adverse events are summarised unevenly across trials.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A tabulation of six MAPS-linked trials (280 participants: four small pilot or phase 2 trials and the two phase 3 trials), without pooling, risk-of-bias tool or certainty rating. Five of six favoured MDMA significantly; by the review's own count, four of six had functional unblinding, all had conflicts of interest with MAPS, four had very small samples, and adverse-event reporting was inconsistent. Several numbers in its tables differ from the trial reports.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the findings support MDMA-AT as a viable treatment option and that it appeared well tolerated (Abstract, p. 1). The Discussion says the trials supported its safe and effective use, calls the two phase 3 trials well designed and sufficient for the FDA's two-trial paradigm, suggesting the treatment could be considered for approval (p. 8), and, while accepting functional unblinding as a valid concern, states without a source that “researchers considered it unlikely that unblinding alone could explain the magnitude and durability” of the gains (p. 9). The main conclusion cites the retracted Mithoefer et al. (2019) among its supporting trials (p. 8). The claim that five studies with long-term follow-up showed maintained or improved gains rests on uncontrolled follow-ups, mostly after open-label crossover (Appendix). The conclusion still calls for larger, more diverse trials and an active placebo (p. 10).

timeline.event: MAPP1, phase 3 trial analysed in the review.
MAPP2, phase 3 trial added by the 2025 rerun of the search.
Retraction, in August 2024, of the pooled phase 2 analyses by Mithoefer et al. (2019) and Jerome et al. (2020), as reported by this review; the notices themselves were not read by this reader.

replication.where_it_stands: The review adds no data and, because of its errors and lack of appraisal, cannot replace the trial reports; it is useful mainly for its inventory, which by May 2025 found no randomized trial of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD without a link to MAPS.

funding.funder: No funding (Funding, p. 10); a librarian ran the database searches as non-financial support (Other information, p. 10).
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors (Disclosure statement, p. 10).
funding.affiliations_note: Psychology Department, Colorado State University – Pueblo (p. 1).

what_would_settle_it: A registered systematic review with meta-analysis of all randomized trials of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD, including trial-registry results and regulatory documents, with duplicate extraction, RoB 2 assessments that address unblinding, pooled effects with intervals, and GRADE certainty ratings.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: The stated criteria are design, condition and intervention only; comparator and outcomes are not specified, and the restriction to trials using the CAPS was added after screening (p. 2).
Randomized trials only, explained as the valid evidence on safety and efficacy (Rationale and objective, p. 2).

Five databases and keywords given, but publication restrictions (peer-reviewed journals, 2002–2022) are not justified and no full strategy, trial registry, regulatory document, reference-list search or expert contact is reported (p. 2).
Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts independently (p. 2); how disagreements were resolved is not stated.

The Methods say only that reviewers created tables; the abstract's statement that data were independently reviewed does not describe duplicate extraction, and several extracted numbers differ from the trial reports.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Exclusions after the first selection are named with reasons (four articles, two retracted analyses and one follow-up), but the 14 earlier exclusions are given only as counts by reason, and the reason for excluding the Bouso et al. (2008) trial departs from the stated criteria (p. 2).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, sample size, CAPS threshold, sex, age, arms and initial doses and number of sessions; country, setting, timing of the primary end point and follow-up length are not tabulated, and some entries are wrong.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No tool was used; Table 5 lists blinding, sample size, diversity, conflicts of interest and bias-reduction steps, but allocation concealment, missing data and selective reporting are not assessed (pp. 7–8).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: MAPS is named for every trial (Table 5; p. 8), though as a conflict of interest rather than as funder.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations section names expectancy, small samples and conflicts of interest (p. 8), but the conclusions call the phase 3 trials well designed and the treatment safe and efficacious, and dismiss unblinding with an unsourced statement (pp. 8–9).
The one discordant trial is attributed speculatively to rater differences (p. 8); differences in comparator (active or inactive placebo), number of sessions and population are not examined.
No quantitative synthesis; the review also does not ask whether registered phase 2 trials without separate publications exist.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding and no conflicts declared (p. 10).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items are not met (2, protocol; 4, search; 9, risk-of-bias assessment) and a fourth (13) is not met, with item 7 only partly met, which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. Beyond the instrument, the review contains many transcription errors (reporting issues) and cites a retracted analysis in its main conclusion. It may be cited for its inventory of published randomized trials up to May 2025 and for its report of the 2024 retractions and the FDA advisory panel's concerns, both second-hand; it should not be cited for any trial result, which should come from the trial reports.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: CINAHL, PubMed, Medline, PsycInfo and the Cochrane Library searched in March 2023 (clinical trials in peer-reviewed journals, 2002–2022) and again in May 2025; 26 unique records, 12 meeting criteria after independent screening by two reviewers, 14 eliminated; the rerun gave 12 more records and one inclusion (MAPP2); four further articles were eliminated, three for secondary outcomes and one trial (Bouso et al., 2008) for using other outcome measures, partly because it was run outside the United States.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Two tabled articles, Mithoefer et al. (2019) and Jerome et al. (2020), were retracted in August 2024 because they included data from a site where a serious ethical violation occurred, identified in Table 1 as MP4, NCT01958593; they are shown in Table 1 but excluded from all calculations, as is the long-term follow-up by Mithoefer et al. (2013).
key_findings.locator: Results › Study and participant characteristics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2); Table 1 and its footnote (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Six trials analysed with 280 participants: 160 (57.1%) in active-dose MDMA arms and 120 (42.9%) given an inactive or active placebo; three trials used an inactive and three a low-dose active placebo; three used two and three used three experimental sessions; mean age 37.2 to 42.0 years; 66.4% female.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study and participant characteristics, 2nd paragraph (starts on p. 2, continues on p. 3); Table 1 (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Efficacy: 5 of 6 trials (83.3%) found a significantly greater CAPS decrease with MDMA; Oehen et al. (2013) found a non-significant decrease. Loss of diagnosis at the primary end point 41.7% to 85.7% in active-dose arms vs 25.0% to 33% in placebo arms, except Oehen et al. (2013), where all 12 still met criteria; Table 2 gives 28 of 42 (67%) for MAPP1 and 37 of 52 (71.2%) for MAPP2 without their placebo results.
key_findings.locator: Efficacy of MDMA-AT for PTSD, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Adverse events: reporting varied substantially between trials and measures; muscle tightness or jaw clenching was among the top three events on MDMA in all six trials and headache the most common on placebo; Table 3 lists, for MAPP1, muscle tightness 29 (63%) vs 5 (11%), decreased appetite 24 (52%) vs 5 (11%), nausea 14 (30%) vs 5 (11%) and substance use 3 (6%) vs 0, and for MAPP2 the values of that trial's Table 2.
key_findings.locator: Safety of MDMA-AT: adverse events (p. 4, right column, and p. 6, left column); Table 3 (pp. 5–6)

key_findings.finding: Suicidality: four trials reported C-SSRS data; lifetime positive ideation 83.7% to 96.4%; in the two phase 3 trials the number with ideation never exceeded baseline in either arm; suicidal behaviour during the study was reported only in a placebo participant (MAPP1).
key_findings.locator: Risk of suicidality (p. 6, right column, to p. 8, left column); Table 4 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Blinding: blinding was maintained or partly maintained in 2 of 6 trials, both with an active placebo; the review states that in the other four, correct guesses by active-dose participants ranged from 90% to 95%, indicating functional unblinding in 66.7% of trials. Table 5 gives 95% of participants correct for Mithoefer et al. (2011), 58.1% to 72.7% for Ot'alora et al. (2018), no formal assessment for MAPP1 and 94.2% (MDMA) and 75% (placebo) for MAPP2.

Limitations named by the review: conflicts of interest with MAPS in all trials (financial support to investigators, study drug, input on design), very small samples (12 to 28) in four trials, limited diversity, and possible expectation bias, observer expectancy and selective reporting.
Dropout: 16.7% (Oehen et al., 2013) and 7.1% (Ot'alora et al., 2018); the review gives 9% for both phase 3 trials, with four dropouts from each arm in MAPP1 and 1 vs 8 in MAPP2.
key_findings.note: MAPP1's report shows 4 of 46 on MDMA and 7 of 44 on placebo not completing treatment (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: FDA advisory panel, as described without a citation: the panel voted against recommending MDMA-AT, concluding that the data did not sufficiently show efficacy and that benefits did not outweigh risks; its concerns included potential functional unblinding, lack of standardized psychotherapy across sites, suicidal ideation, cardiovascular risk and potential misuse; the review adds that an ethical violation in one trial, publicly documented on YouTube, led to the retraction of multiple articles.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph starting on p. 9 (right column)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: the trials support MDMA-AT as potentially safe and efficacious; the two phase 3 trials meet the FDA's minimum two-trial paradigm; functional unblinding is a valid concern but said to be unlikely to explain the gains; future trials should be larger and more diverse, track sessions, drug effects, adverse events, suicidality and misuse more consistently, and consider an active placebo.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 8) and 3rd paragraph starting on p. 9; Conclusion and future implications (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Not registered, no protocol, no funding, no declared conflicts of interest.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says seven randomized trials with 280 participants were identified and six were analysed for efficacy; the Results analyse six trials, whose sample sizes (20, 12, 28, 26, 90, 104) alone sum to 280.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the seventh is apparently the excluded long-term follow-up, which is not a separate trial.

reporting_issues.issue: The stated placebo range for loss of diagnosis, 25.0% to 33.3%, omits MAPP2's placebo result of 47.6% (20 of 42), and Table 2 gives neither phase 3 trial's placebo figure (MAPP1: 32%, 12 of 37).
reporting_issues.consequence: The contrast between arms is overstated; in MAPP2 nearly half of placebo completers lost the diagnosis.

reporting_issues.issue: The review states that correct guesses by active-dose participants ranged from 90% to 95% in four trials, but its own Table 5 gives 58.1% for one of them (Ot'alora et al., 2018) and no rate for MAPP1, which did not assess blinding.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only two trials support the stated range; the unblinding conclusion is still supported by the MAPP2 survey and the 2011 pilot.

reporting_issues.issue: MAPP1's dropout is given as 9% with four dropouts from each arm, but the trial report shows 4 of 46 on MDMA and 7 of 44 on placebo not completing treatment (12% of 90), plus one withdrawal before dosing.
reporting_issues.consequence: The between-arm difference in MAPP1 dropout is hidden.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 gives MAPP1's suicidality events of special interest as three suicidal ideation on MDMA and two ideation plus one self-harm on placebo (three, not the five stated); the trial's Table 2 gives two ideation and one self-harm with ideation on MDMA, and three ideation and two with suicidal behaviour or self-harm on placebo. For MAPP2, Table 4 gives a baseline rate of 15 of 104 (14.4%), which does not appear in the trial report, and lists as during-study values the 13 of 53 and 12 of 51 that the trial reports at the final preparation session.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the trial reports for suicidality figures.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives MAPP1 events in 4 participants as 5% (4 of 46 is 8.7%) in four rows, and muscle tightness as 29 vs 5, while the trial registry gives 28 vs 6 (over a longer window); the review's source for MAPP1's adverse events is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Percentages in the table cannot be relied on.

reporting_issues.issue: The text defines the 160 active-dose participants by an initial-dose threshold that would also take in one trial's active-placebo arm, which the count excludes; Tables 1 and 2 give different doses for that active placebo; and Table 1 gives the phase 3 trials only their first-session initial dose (see the exposure field).
reporting_issues.consequence: The tabulated exposure of the phase 3 trials is incomplete; use the trial reports.

reporting_issues.issue: Long-term follow-up results are summarised as 41.6% to 100% no longer meeting criteria 12 months or longer after the study, but the 100% is the 2011 pilot's 7 of 7 at 2 months (Table 2); the follow-ups mostly came after open-label crossover, so no placebo group remained.
reporting_issues.consequence: The durability statement in the abstract and Discussion is not supported as written.

reporting_issues.issue: The main conclusion cites Mithoefer et al. (2019), one of the two retracted analyses the review says it excluded; the review names the retracting journal as the Journal of Psychopharmacology, while the DOIs it gives and its reference list place both articles in Psychopharmacology.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the retractions from the notices (Crossref), not from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The Appendix says about 61% of MAPP2 participants were ethnically diverse, which is the sum of two overlapping percentages (33.7% other than White and 26.9% Hispanic or Latino).

Sex counts differ between Table 1 and Table 5 for three studies (Oehen et al., 2013: 2 M, 10 F vs 3 M, 7 F; Ot'alora et al., 2018: 9 M, 19 F vs 9 M, 16 F; Mithoefer et al., 2013: 3 M, 16 F vs 3 M, 13 F); the text says three studies reported treatment-related adverse events but names two.
reporting_issues.page: pp. 3, 4, 7 (Tables 1 and 5; Safety of MDMA-AT, 1st paragraph)

reporting_issues.issue: The reference list names the journal of both phase 3 trials as Naturopathic Medicine; unresolved typesetting queries (marked AQ) remain in the published Appendix; the FDA is called the Federal Drug Administration, and the abstract says the FDA voted, while the Discussion describes an advisory panel vote, for which no source is cited.
reporting_issues.consequence: Signs of limited editorial checking; the advisory panel's vote and concerns should be taken from primary regulatory sources.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1–13 (PDFs/MDMA/Brett_2025_MDMAATSystematicReview.pdf), all pages; Tables 1–5 checked on rendered pages.
